name: Mauve
lede: Mauve is the French name of the mallow flower, borrowed for a soft greyish purple; in 1856 an 18-year-old chemist made a coal-tar dye that took the name and turned it into a craze.

sections.title: A flower's name
sections.body:
*Mauve* is the French word for the common mallow, and the color is its petal color [1][2]. English took it over in the 1850s, and Victorians said it the French way, closer to "morv" [1][2]. In the old language of flowers, the mallow stood for mildness [17], which suits the color as most people now use the word: a soft, greyish pink-purple, lighter and duller than [[purple]] and less blue than [[lilac]].

The swatch here is the modern dictionary mauve, ISCC-NBS block 217 [16]. It is not the color of 1856 [7]. Perkin's dye was a vivid, saturated purple, and the word has drifted paler and greyer since; Garfield notes that mauve has never been one fixed color, running from lilac to lush purple [2][4]. Its nearest named neighbors today are [[eupatorium-purple]], [[mountbatten-pink]] and [[opera-mauve]] [16].

sections.title: A fashion before the dye
sections.body:
The popular story has Perkin's dye launching the fashion, but the order was really the reverse [3][5]. A purple from lichens, sold as French purple, was hugely popular in the 1850s, and it is the reason the word mauve moved from naming a dye to naming a color [6]. The Paris fashion for mauve took hold during late 1857 and crossed to London in 1858, and it ran at first on French lichen purples and murexide, a purple made from bird guano [2][3]. In Britain murexide was sold as Roman purple; the old claim that it came from serpent excrement is a myth [3][7].

Empress Eugénie's fondness for the color was noted in late 1857, and in January 1858 Queen Victoria wore mauve velvet to her daughter's wedding [2][8]. Perkin's aniline purple rode a wave that was already rising [5].

sections.title: Perkin's purple
sections.body:
At Easter 1856 William Henry Perkin, eighteen years old and a student of August Hofmann, was working in a makeshift laboratory at home [3][7]. He was trying to make quinine, the malaria drug, from a coal-tar chemical called allyltoluidine, and got only a reddish powder [7]. He tried again with plain aniline and potassium dichromate, and this time the flask held a black sludge [3][7]. Washed with spirits of wine, about five per cent of it gave up a purple that dyed silk and stood up to light [7][3]. Quinine itself was not synthesized until 1944 [9].

It was not luck alone. Perkin's later admirers called mauve the least accidental of discoveries, given how systematically he chased the residue, though *Nature* suggested in 1956 that someone else would have found aniline dyes within a few years [10]. A later legend says he got the idea from the rainbow film of tar on a puddle; at the 1906 jubilee the chemist Raphael Meldola denied it outright [11].

Perkin patented the process in August 1856, at an age when patents were normally granted only to adults [7]. His father put up the money for a factory at Greenford Green, near Harrow, which opened in 1857 [12]. The yields were tiny: about a hundred pounds of coal gave a quarter of an ounce of dye [12][8]. He first sold it as Tyrian purple, borrowing the prestige of the imperial shellfish dye, and by 1859 had switched to the French fashion name, mauve; in the journals he called the compound mauveine [3][7][1].

sections.title: Mauve measles
sections.body:
By 1859 the color was everywhere [5]. *Punch* that August joked about an epidemic of "mauve measles" sweeping London [2][3]. The word first appeared in *The Times* that July, in a notice about a lost parasol [2]. Within about two years the boom was over, and buyers moved on to the next aniline sensations, magenta first among them [2]. At the 1862 International Exhibition Perkin and Sons still showed off a pillar of solid mauve [12].

The color then found a quieter, longer career in mourning. Victorian etiquette moved a widow from black through grey or mauve in the last months of mourning [13][14]. Queen Victoria herself had exchanged black for mauve less than four years after Prince Albert died [12], and mauve was still allowed for half-mourning at the British court around 1952 [15].

sections.title: What mauve started
sections.body:
Perkin's discovery is usually summed up as the first aniline dye, and that is the safe description [3][7][18]. Calling it the first synthetic dye is wrong: picric acid, a coal-tar yellow, was dyeing silk in Lyon from 1845 [3]. Whether mauve was at least the first *commercial* synthetic dye is something the books disagree on, Garfield saying yes and Ball pointing to picric acid [7][3][18].

What is not in doubt is what followed. Aniline reds, violets and blues came within a few years, and the small dye works that made them grew into BASF, Bayer and Ciba [1][6]. By the mauve jubilee in 1906 about two thousand artificial colors existed [7]. Biologists borrowed the new dyes to stain cells; mauve was among the first used, in the early 1860s [19].

sections.title: Mauve in paint and words
sections.body:
Painters mostly mixed their mauves rather than buying one. The Impressionists glazed cobalt or ultramarine with a red lake, and used the new cobalt and manganese violets less often [20]. In Monet's *Lavacourt under Snow*, the blue snow is tinted mauve with ultramarine and red lake [20].

Writers reached for the word as soon as it existed. Proust described asparagus stippled in mauve and azure [21], and Huysmans listed mauve among the soft derivatives of blue that suit dreamers [21].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
As a painted color the dusty modern mauve is rare. In our archive of 23,531 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only five works [22]. Four of them date from 1892 to 1913: Gauguin's *Fatata te Miti*, Kirchner's *Two Girls under an Umbrella*, Klimt's *The Maiden* and an Indian goddess painting of about 1900 [22]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [22].

The word is easier to date than the paint. In Google Books, *mauve* is almost absent before the late 1850s, jumps to about 40 per cent of its eventual peak by 1860, and peaks around 1925 [23]. It is one of the few color words whose birth you can see in the data.
